78: Our kitchen is the first decision that shapes everything else, and we do not build one. A full-service off-site caterer still needs a permitted kitchen, so we rent time in a shared commissary kitchen that already holds the health permit: cooking hours, dry and cold storage and a parking spot for the van, budgeted at {{alquiler_mes}} per month in the example case. Published hourly rates for shared kitchens typically run from $15 to $45 depending on the city and the equipment, so we compare at least three commissaries on price, hours that actually fit a Saturday-heavy schedule, walk-in and freezer space, loading access and how early we can get in on event days. Before paying a deposit we sign a written commissary agreement that spells out our hours, our shelves and refrigeration, cleaning duties, insurance requirements and notice for ending the arrangement. Most county health departments want to see that agreement, and so will a lender. This choice keeps the up-front investment far below what a leased, built-out production kitchen would cost, and it lets us scale hours up in wedding season and down in January.
79: Equipment follows the same logic: own what travels, rent what does not. We buy one used refrigerated cargo van ({{inv_vehiculo}}) and add a reliable refrigeration unit with professional installation ({{inv_frio}}), because a van that cannot hold temperature is a liability, not an asset. Chafing dishes, insulated food carriers and serving ware ({{inv_menaje_servicio}}) are ours too, since we use them at nearly every event. Linens, tables, chairs, glassware and tents come from local party rental companies and are passed through in the quote, so we never carry inventory we use twice a year. That keeps cash free for what clients actually taste and see.
80: Every event follows the same six phases, and the schedule is written down. Around three weeks out we send a briefing form covering guest count, dietary needs, style of service, venue and budget. About two weeks out we visit the venue to check power, water, access, kitchen space and load-in times. In the last week we place orders with suppliers, buying perishables as late as the menu allows. The day before, we prep and pack in the commissary; on event day we load the van, drive, set up in 60 to 90 minutes and serve. Within 24 to 48 hours we collect equipment, close the books on the event and invoice any remaining balance.
81: Food safety does not pause when the food leaves the kitchen. Hot food is held at 135 F or above and cold food at 41 F or below, and we log temperatures at loading, on arrival and at the end of service. Cold items travel in the refrigerated van or in insulated carriers with verified ice packs, hot items in preheated carriers, and nothing sits in the danger zone for more than the time our HACCP-based plan allows. Allergens are handled on the event sheet: every guest with a restriction is named in the briefing, dishes are labeled at the station, and prep for those dishes is separated and documented. A chef-attended station is also our best allergy control, because the person serving can answer questions on the spot.
82: We buy from one broadline distributor for staples and a short list of specialists for produce, proteins and bakery, with a backup for each so a missed delivery never cancels a menu. Party rentals are ordered per event from a small set of local companies, and their delivery times are written into the event sheet. The van itself gets a simple routine: oil, tires, brakes and refrigeration service on a calendar, a monthly pre-trip checklist and a fuel and maintenance line in the P&L. A breakdown on a Saturday is the single most expensive operating failure we can have, so preventive maintenance is cheaper than any rescue.
85: The team is small, and each role has a clear job. The owner is executive chef and head of sales, which means writing proposals, running tastings and leading the kitchen on the biggest events. A sous chef or kitchen lead runs production at the commissary and covers the owner at events. A pool of event staff, made up of servers, bartenders and attendants, is scheduled per event. A prep cook who also drives completes the core crew and handles loading, deliveries and cleanup. As volume grows, the first additions are more event staff hours and a second prep shift, not more fixed salaries.
86: The fixed crew costs {{personal_a1}} in year 1, including employer payroll taxes, which is {{personal_pct}} of sales. That figure covers the owner's draw, the sous chef, the prep cook and driver, and the event staff hours the workbook schedules for the year-1 volume. We lock in the fixed portion early because the people who run the kitchen are the ones who protect quality, and we let the variable portion move with the calendar. In the workbook, the {{personal_pct}} sits inside the labor benchmark we use for the plan, and you can test any change in pay or headcount directly on the "Staffing" tab.
87: Event staff are the variable cost that moves with the calendar. Each event needs about {{horas_evento}} hours of coverage, from production through loading, service and pack-down, and an average of {{personas_evento}} people, so a heavier month costs more labor and a quiet month costs less. The workbook compares the hours scheduled with the hours required and reports {{cobertura_horas}} coverage. As a Kit estimate, plated service needs roughly one server for every 10 to 12 guests, while buffets and stations stretch to 20 to 25 guests per server. We set staffing from the style we quote, never from habit, and we write it into the proposal.
88: We hire event staff as W-2 employees. Servers and bartenders at private events work under our direction, on our schedule, with our equipment, which is the profile that federal rules under the Fair Labor Standards Act treat as employment, and in California the ABC test under AB5 presumes it. Calling them independent contractors may look cheaper, but misclassification can bring back taxes, penalties and claims, and it can undo a loan application. Payroll taxes and benefits add {{cargas_pct}} to wages in the model, and workers' compensation is required in nearly every state. We pay at least the highest of the federal, state and local minimum wage, which the workbook sets against the federal floor of {{salario_minimo_federal}} for full-time work. Check your state and city rules, because many are higher.
89: Training is part of the plan, not an extra. At least one person on every event holds a Certified Food Protection Manager credential such as ServSafe, and every food handler carries the card your state or county requires. Anyone who pours alcohol at a client-supplied bar holds an alcohol server certification such as TIPS or ServSafe Alcohol, or the state equivalent. Before the first event of the season we run a short service protocol: how to greet guests, how to answer allergy questions, when to alert the chef, how to break down a station and how to handle a complaint on the spot. Certificates are filed with the commissary and checked at renewal time. The workbook carries the cost of these courses on its own line.
90: Pay the service charge and the gratuity differently, because the IRS does. Under IRS Revenue Ruling 2012-18, a mandatory service charge that the client must pay is treated as wages to the staff who receive it, so payroll taxes apply. A tip is voluntary, the amount is up to the guest and the recipient is the guest's choice. We list the service charge and any voluntary gratuity on separate lines of the quote, we say plainly what each pays for, and we distribute gratuities to the event staff according to a written policy. Whether the service charge itself is subject to sales tax depends on your state, which is covered in the legal section.
93: Taken together, the example case describes a viable small business. Year-1 revenue reaches {{ventas_a1}} with a gross margin of {{margen_bruto_pct}}, and EBITDA comes to {{ebitda_a1}}, or {{ebitda_pct_a1}} of sales. Those are planning figures from the Excel workbook of this kit, not a forecast. They hold only while your events per year, price per guest and guests per event are realistic for your area, and the "0. Assumptions" tab is where you change them.
94: Start-up costs in the example are built from the lines you can price today. The refrigerated van costs {{inv_vehiculo}}, its upfit {{inv_adaptacion}} and its refrigeration unit {{inv_frio}}. Kitchen and refrigeration equipment adds {{inv_equipo_cocina}}, chafing dishes, carriers and serving ware {{inv_menaje_servicio}}, first-year permits and licenses {{inv_permisos}}, launch marketing {{inv_lanzamiento}} and opening inventory {{inv_stock}}. Together with the remaining lines, such as portable cooking and power, storage fit-out, legal and software, capex totals {{capex}}. On top of that comes a working capital reserve of {{fondo_maniobra}}, which brings the total investment to {{inversion_total}} and the cash needed at opening to {{necesidad_caja}}. The owner puts in {{fondos_propios}}, and a loan of {{prestamo}} covers the rest, at {{tipo_prestamo}} nominal interest over {{plazo_prestamo}} years. The plan is lender-ready, but approval is never guaranteed.
95: Revenue grows with the number of events, not with price. The example moves from {{ventas_a1}} in year 1 to {{ventas_a2}} in year 2 and {{ventas_a3}} in year 3, because events per year grow by {{crecimiento_a2}} and {{crecimiento_a3}} while the price per guest and the guest count stay steady. Net profit follows at {{resultado_neto_a1}}, {{resultado_neto_a2}} and {{resultado_neto_a3}}, after loan interest, depreciation and income tax at an effective rate of {{impuesto_beneficios}}.
96: Costs are set against reference ranges. Food cost on food sales is {{food_cost_comida}}, and total cost of goods is {{cogs_pct}} of sales, with disposables at {{consumibles_pct}}. Labor is {{personal_pct}}, and the commissary and van parking {{ocupacion_pct}}. Published benchmarks put catering food cost at 28-35%, labor at 25-35% and net margin at 7-8% on average, according to Galley Solutions and ItsaCheckmate. The workbook's own thresholds are editable estimates, so adjust them for your menu and market.
97: The break-even is measured in events per year. The business covers its accounting costs at {{equilibrio_eventos}} events and its cash costs at {{equilibrio_caja_eventos}} events, compared with {{eventos_a1}} events in the plan, which leaves a margin of safety of {{holgura_caja_pct}}. The two numbers come out close because depreciation, which is a cost but not a cash outflow, and loan principal repayments, which are cash outflows but not expenses, roughly offset each other. If you are far below that point, raise price or event volume before you spend more.
98: Cash is where a caterer can fail even when the profit looks fine. Corporate clients often pay after {{cobro_dias}} days on average, while food, labor and rentals are paid before the event. In the example the lowest cash balance in year 1 is {{saldo_minimo}}, reached in month {{mes_saldo_minimo}}, the project payback before debt is {{payback}} and the lowest DSCR over the loan term is {{dscr_min}}, against a typical lender guideline of {{dscr_objetivo}}. The model does not count deposits. In real life, a 25-50% deposit at signing improves cash, so treat the model as the cautious case.
99: Three scenarios show how fast the numbers move. The pessimistic case assumes {{pesimista_eventos}} events at {{pesimista_precio}} per guest and {{pesimista_invitados}} guests per event, which gives revenue of {{pesimista_ventas}} and a pre-tax result of {{pesimista_resultado}}, with estimated year-1 closing cash of {{pesimista_caja}}. That is the honest warning of the plan: in a weak year, cash can run out before profit does, so a credit line or a larger reserve matters. The optimistic case reaches {{optimista_ventas}} and a pre-tax result of {{optimista_resultado}}. In the pessimistic case, labor cost also falls as events fall, because event staff are paid per event, which softens the result but does not remove the risk.
102: You cannot run a catering business from your home kitchen. The FDA Food Code counts a catering operation among food establishments, and California, for example, requires caterers to prepare food in a permitted kitchen under a written agreement and prohibits preparation at home, according to the environmental health guidance of one California county (eldoradocounty.ca.gov). Cottage food laws only cover certain shelf-stable foods sold directly to consumers, and California's MEHKO program for home kitchens does not allow catering. That is why this plan rents a shared commissary kitchen, and why your first legal step is a signed agreement with one, not a business license.
103: With the kitchen secured, the next layer is the local health permit. Expect to apply to your county health department for a catering or food facility permit, pay an annual fee and pass an inspection of your commissary and your van. A plan review is only needed if you lease your own kitchen. At least one person should hold a Certified Food Protection Manager certificate such as ServSafe, and food handlers need the card your state or county requires. Write a food safety plan based on HACCP principles and train on the nine major allergens, which include sesame since 2023. Requirements and fees vary by county, so call yours before you spend.
104: Event permits are a separate step. A catering permit generally does not cover community or public events, where you usually need a Temporary Food Facility or temporary event permit, issued per event and often with a deadline. If the plan uses open flame, chafing fuel or a tent, check with the local fire marshal. Many venues also require a certificate of insurance and sometimes ask to be named as an additional insured, so ask the venue manager what they require before you quote.
105: By default, the caterer does not sell alcohol. Doing so takes an on-sale license plus a caterer's permit, such as the Caterer's Permit in Texas or the Type 58 license in California, usually with an authorization for each event. The usual model is simpler: the client buys the alcohol, and bartenders certified in your state, for example through TIPS or TABC, serve it under your liquor liability coverage. Getting your own license is an option for later, and it brings dram shop liability, so speak with a licensed attorney first.
106: Sales tax is where small caterers get surprised. In many states it applies to the whole catering invoice, including food, staff and rentals, as California's tax agency states for caterers, and New York treats a caterer's charges for food, beverages and services as taxable. Whether a service charge is taxed depends on the state: in California a mandatory one is taxable, in New York a separate gratuity paid fully to staff is not, and in Texas it is excluded only when it is stated separately, within a limit, and paid to qualifying employees. Under IRS Revenue Ruling 2012-18, a mandatory service charge is wages, not a tip. Register for a seller's permit in your state; the workbook uses an example sales tax rate of {{sales_tax}}.
107: Hiring and insurance come next. Servers and bartenders at events are almost always employees, so plan on W-2 payroll, workers' compensation, Form I-9, Form W-4 and your state's new-hire reporting. Misclassifying them as contractors is a real risk under the FLSA, and California's AB5 presumes employment. For coverage, plan on general liability or a business owner's policy, commercial auto for the van and liquor liability if staff serve alcohol. The example budgets {{seguros_anual}} per year, and Insureon publishes average prices by policy, so ask for quotes from an agent who knows caterers.
108: The van is registered and titled with your state DMV and needs commercial auto insurance. A commercial driver's license is only required at a gross vehicle weight rating of 26,001 lb or more, which a cargo van does not reach. If you operate in the UK, the rules differ: register your food business with the local council at least 28 days before you start, expect a Food Hygiene Rating from 0 to 5, charge VAT at 20% on catering for events and functions under HMRC VAT Notice 709/1, use a Temporary Event Notice at £21 if you serve alcohol without a premises licence, and declare the 14 listed allergens.
111: The plan holds together because of how it is built. There is no kitchen to lease and build out, only shared time in a permitted commissary, and one refrigerated van instead of a fleet. Two demand engines balance each other: corporate clients fill the week with drop-offs, lunch buffets, receptions and holiday parties, and private clients fill the weekends with weddings, rehearsal dinners and milestone celebrations. Chef-attended stations give the brand something to be known for and a price that is not set by the cheapest quote in the marketplace. If the numbers are tested honestly, this is a business you can start with a bounded investment and grow event by event.
112: Know the risks before you sign anything. Last-minute cancellations are handled by a deposit of 25-50% at signing and a written cancellation schedule, and no date is held without both. Foodborne illness is prevented by an HACCP-based plan, temperature logs and insurance. A van breakdown is covered by maintenance, a backup refrigerated option and a relationship with the commissary. Late-paying companies are managed by deposits, clear terms and card or ACH payment. A staff shortage is handled by a bench of trained event staff. Allergic reactions are prevented by written briefings and labeled stations, and rain at an outdoor event by a documented plan B and a tent partner.
113: Our strengths come from focus. We sell a small number of things well: stations that feel like entertainment, run by a chef who stays at the station. We keep fixed costs low through a shared kitchen and a single van, so a slow month hurts less. We are honest in proposals about what the quote includes and what the service charge pays for. And we run on documented procedures, so quality does not depend on one heroic weekend.
114: The roadmap follows the six phases of the checklist that comes with this kit. In "Phase 1 - Business Setup" you form the LLC, open the bank account, get insurance quotes and register for the seller's permit. "Phase 2 - Kitchen, Van, Permits" covers the commissary agreement, the health permit and the van. "Phase 3 - Equipment" buys the serving ware, carriers and portable cooking gear. "Phase 4 - Staff" sets up payroll, certifications and your event staff pool. "Phase 5 - Marketing" builds the website, listings and first tastings. "Phase 6 - First 90 Days" runs your first events and reviews every one. Do not move to the next phase while the permits of the current one are open.
115: Measure a few things every week, and do not wait for the accountant. Track events booked per month and the conversion rate of proposals into signed contracts. Track the average price per guest against the plan figure of {{precio_invitado}}, food cost against {{food_cost_comida}}, and labor per event against {{horas_evento}} hours and {{personas_evento}} people. Track cancellations, the share of repeat corporate clients and the number of reviews collected after each event. If two or three of these drift for a month, fix them before you add events.
116: Looking three years ahead, the plan is to grow the recurring corporate base, which smooths the week and lowers selling cost per event, as events rise from {{eventos_a1}} to {{eventos_a3}}. A second van becomes sensible when the commissary calendar and the cash balance both support it, and not sooner. A kitchen of your own is a later decision again, taken only when your hours at the commissary are consistently full and a lease costs less than the hours you are renting. Each step is paid from cash flow, so the business does not depend on bigger loans.
117: The next steps are simple and in order. Open the Excel workbook and replace the example assumptions with your own events, price per guest and guest count. Use the pricing calculator to turn that into quotes you can send, with the service charge and gratuity on separate lines. Then work through the startup checklist one phase at a time. This plan is a planning tool, not legal or tax advice, so confirm permits, taxes and insurance with your accountant, your county and your attorney before you commit money.
